essays.prompt: In her November 2019 Ted Talk, "The Danger of a Single Story," Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie warned viewers against assigning people a "single story" through assumptions about their nationality, appearance, or background. Discuss a time when someone defined you by a single story. What challenges did this present and how did you overcome them? (400 words)
essays.essay:
Harry Potter glasses-wearing Asian girl who plays piano and tutors at a math center. Can it get any more stereotypical? In a way, I don't blame people for assuming stories about me that fit the maladaptive stereotypes of an Asian girl in the Bay Area. But it didn't make life easier.

A question that has always been at the back of my mind is why do I have to be good at everything? Why do people assume I have to be good at everything? Of course, no one is good at everything. But everything people expected of me included sports, academics, arts, socializing, and so much more. During middle school, there had been several distinct instances in which I was grouped under that umbrella. A mutual friend had once approached me with papers in hand, asking for help on their history homework, which I was struggling with at the time. I had peers come up to me asking about which church I go to (I'm not religious). The slightly backhanded comments piled up to the point where I thought I needed to be just like that, that there was no room for me to try to be anyone else because of this defining story. Because what was the point of being someone else if that is all people were to view me as? Just a shadow behind the common stereotype.

Thankfully, that mindset soon faded once I started to find the little things that mattered to me, not to anyone else. Picking up things such as trying out the guitar, cooking with my grandmother, learning HTML, and even longboarding assisted me in breaking out of this harmful mindset. It took a lot longer to overcome most of my social anxiety that came with unfortunate interactions, but finding new interests fueled me to be someone new. Someone better.

I am still an Asian girl, wearing the same Harry Potter glasses who plays piano and tutors at a math center in the Bay Area. But that single story has depth only dedicated readers will discover. Now I know how to make silly websites, take digital art commissions, cook spaghetti, and somewhat longboard down the hill I grew up on. Yes, I am a bit of a stereotype, but I know I am so much more.

essays.prompt: What about being a student at Boston University most excites you? (250 words)
essays.essay:
With the luxury of Boston University's surroundings; its progressive socio-political climate; BU's global recognition pertaining to its research facilities; the access to groundbreaking technological advances and medicinal research; and Massachusetts's fast-paced urban lifestyle - I find myself already readying into adapting into the next thrilling experience of my life.

As I have always been a curious girl (and an aspiring physician) who found being challenged by new surroundings exhilarating, I'm always prepared to advance my understanding of neuroscience and psychology in a place whose foremost focus is academic excellence. BU's Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP) specifically, is also a great way to maximize our learning experience, challenging all undergraduates to perform even better and connect us with good future employers.

One checking of BU's website informing me about its emphasis on diversity/inclusion most certainly helps, too. The safe and beautiful environment, the many student housing blocks, the prospect of joining great academic clubs and networking with the postgraduates while being at the center of innovation - these were just a few of the things that convince me that BU is the place where I could truly excel at.

BU simply boasts all the things where I could further my interests in medicine, scientific research, and healthcare work. I have no doubt BU is also the perfect place for me to find and expound on strategic plans when it comes to future career decisions. And I hope I will be allowed to find new meaningful experiences and add color to the campus's already-vibrant surroundings.

essays.prompt: At Brown, you will learn as much from your peers outside the classroom as in academic spaces. How will you contribute to the Brown community? (250 words)
essays.essay:
As I have always been a curious girl who found being challenged by new surroundings exhilarating, I'm always prepared to advance my understanding of neurosciences in a place whose foremost focus is academic excellence. Having visited the campus during my brief stay in Rhode Island, I found the students and faculty members wandering about and being lively, and thought to myself, "How could I add more color to this esteemed campus?"

Living in Southern California, I have always found myself to be a person who took advantage of every leadership opportunity, and testing as many waters as possible. I flat-out do not believe in the phrase "jack of all trades, master of none". Or, at least, I don't want to be boxed in by such conditions. While I utilized most of my time doing research work, I also found great joy studying programming languages with my friends who took different courses. I have also learned how to use and enjoy fashion in creating unique and personal pieces of clothing using raw materials. I try to be as well-rounded in every fundamental skill set in order to outperform my age and societal limitations.

During my stay for college, I aspire to do just the same - taking with me my determination of learning about new cultures and local customs while sharing my personal core principles of curiosity and diplomatic nature. At Brown, I hope I will be allowed to find new meaningful experiences and add more definition to the campus's already-vibrant surroundings.

essays.prompt: Please briefly elaborate on one of your extracurricular activities or work experiences. (150 words)
essays.essay: I started being the representative for the Society for Neuroscience Speaker Events at my high school in 2016 and have been promoting awareness for neuroscience as a field and a possible career path at our school. In this post, I reached out to many students who were academically brilliant but weren't sure just yet which field they wanted to major in after graduating high school. It seems daunting to a 12 year old when being asked where they see themselves when they finally join the work force as we were all just discovering who we are as people. But with a good team, we found and fostered candidates that were equally dedicated to biology and psychology. We then started taking several steps by strategically placing ourselves in activities such as attending neuroscience-related conventions where we could hobnob with professionals in Southern California and get grounded advice in career choices.

essays.prompt: Tell us about something that is meaningful to you and why. (100 to 250 words)
essays.essay:
In a country where healthcare is not easily affordable and is in a constant debate as to whether being properly or not properly supported, I would like to dedicate my future research into finding substantial data that may one day alleviate conditions and illnesses that face the same dilemma in terms of general support, funding, staffing, and finding cheaper alternatives to costly treatments.

Growing up in a state with an ever-shifting political climate, I've always been aware of many debates and public outcries that seem to divide the population. Now that I'm well within maturation, I've been finding myself more engaged on serious topics such as changes in state policies.

One good instance of this was how, as a child, I've always been in opposition with all the things our society has labeled "vices", parroting the views of my elders. These beliefs were challenged during the summer of 2018 when I started doing community service in a Veterans Affairs hospital. There, most tasks involved assisting veterans into readjusting to society. We monitored which treatments worked with patients who were going through severe PTSD, and saw how easier access to prescription cannabinoids helped veterans regain their appetite and, in certain ways, their will to live.

After seeing a lot of patients respond more positively to the recently-made-legal prescriptions, I realized these findings surpassed the strict, automatic judgment that were once politically passed around. I learned that we could push for better treatment options without having to resort into anything prejudicial.

essays.prompt: Identify and describe two STEM-related experiences from your high school years, either in or out of the classroom, and tell us how and why they activated your curiosity. STEM experience/activity #1 (200 words)
essays.essay:
During the summer of Freshman year, I joined a social media startup called Revoteen. Prior to this, I was working on basic projects and had no real-world programming experience. I saw Revoteen as a wonderful opportunity to develop my knowledge in full stack development, while also enhancing my collaboration skills.

It was a completely different experience working with a team of programmers, writing efficient code, and deploying it to the cloud. I was able to delve deeper into the inner workings of JavaScript and learn about frameworks such as Next.js. Revoteen is the reason that JavaScript is my favorite language today.

I learned about how code is shipped to the production environment and how to write effective tests to ensure that this code is not erroneous. It brought me joy each time I saw the "Deploy Successful" message as I knew that my feature was contributing to the overall success of the application.

Revoteen's charismatic work environment coupled with their desire to innovate and develop creative solutions was the reason I became so attached to the company. Each day, I was ecstatic to work on a feature. I was determined to fix any bug or error that stood in my way. It taught me essential skills that will undoubtedly help me in my career as a programmer.

essays.prompt: Identify and describe two STEM-related experiences from your high school years, either in or out of the classroom, and tell us how and why they activated your curiosity. STEM experience/activity #2 (200 words)
essays.essay:
Aside from my desire to work on real codebases, I am also passionate about competitive programming which strengthens my critical thinking skills. While solving complex problems using code may seem boring to many, it was intriguing to me as I realized how these algorithms could be used in the real world.

Besides the extreme joy I found when successfully completing a problem, I love competitive programming since the solutions to problems can be used in real world applications. Every time I look at Google Maps while on the road, I think about pathfinding algorithms such as Flood-Fill, BFS, Dijkstra's, and A-Star. I continually ponder how these apps are calculating the shortest path. Maybe they were using a combination of these weighted algorithms but also taking into account data from other devices. Even games such as Wordle rely on data structures like HashMaps in order for their game to work efficiently.

Participating in competitions such as the Facebook Hackercup, Google Code Jam, and most importantly USACO, I learned how to think critically, recognize frequent patterns, and utilize a variety of algorithms.

essays.prompt: Please indicate your proposed area of interest at Caltech. Why did you choose that area of interest? (200 words)
essays.essay:
"Daddy, how much longer until we reach?" I asked with impatience, my hunger growing as the GPS displayed an ever-changing ETA. I became increasingly frustrated, and I was suspicious that Google Maps was giving us slow routes. "I build a better map," my seven-year-old self frustratedly said from the back seat, completely unaware of the intricate operations occurring behind the screen. My dad chuckled at my grammar but surprisingly reassured me that I could build a better product one day. This interaction ignited a curiosity not only for Google Maps but for all applications.

This curiosity inspired me to pursue a path in computer science, where I discovered a passion for competitive programming and full-stack development. I furthered my skills in this area by creating award-winning applications, participating in various competitions, and leading programming initiatives. Each solved problem felt like I was uncovering hidden treasures, my heart racing as I implemented the complex logic. The awards on my shelf had a unique glow, serving as a testament to my relentless effort and innovation. As I continued to learn, stumbling across pathfinding algorithms like Dijkstra's, I came to a realization: "Oh, so that's how Google Maps works."

My experiences at Caltech will reinforce my decision to pursue computer science. With its extensive resources and exceptional faculties, I believe that I can significantly expand my knowledge, uncovering the limitless possibilities of computer science. At Caltech, I know that one day I can make my dad proud by building the "better Google Maps."

essays.prompt: Most students choose their intended major or area of study based on a passion or inspiration that's developed over time – what passion or inspiration led you to choose this area of study? (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
With the addition of the final line, my React.js sorting visualizer was complete. My program allows people to physically observe how sorting algorithms such as merge and bubble sort work. The pure bliss I felt when I clicked the sort button and witnessed the teal array bars elegantly rearrange was unlike any other. With my hands in the air and a wide smile on my face, I jubilantly exclaimed in delight.

Following that achievement, my passion for programming led me to new horizons, and I participated in the Congressional App Challenge hosted by the U.S. House of Representatives. At this competition, we wanted to construct an application to help victims of sexual harassment. We worked day and night to develop a product that uses natural language processing and optical character recognition to identify instances of sexual exploitation through screenshots. We also created a database to track offenders. The thrill of designing the webpage and React components made me feel like a painter adding vibrant strokes to a canvas. When I saw the text being parsed from the image successfully, I felt an overwhelming sense of accomplishment. Watching our model correctly predict each image was not just a technical feat but an emotional experience, knowing that we were creating a tool to help others. When I saw the 1st place award, I rejoiced in happiness, and I knew that my path in computer science was a way to make a real impact on people's lives.

This passion propels me forward, knowing that every line of code is a step towards a future where technology is used for good. The triumph in successfully addressing a real-world issue through programming has defined my journey. I am eager to continue on this path of discovery and positive impact at Carnegie Mellon University.

essays.promptLabel: Passion for area of study (business analytics)
essays.prompt: Most students choose their intended major or area of study based on a passion or inspiration that's developed over time – what passion or inspiration led you to choose this area of study? (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
It was 8PM and I was playing Fortnite with a friend. In this game, we chatted about making money in the summer and using our time more productively. We watched influencers on social media earning consistent streams of income by starting businesses and we felt inspired to try our own car detailing business.

Finding capital to start this business was a tough effort. We set up lemonade stands and persuaded our families to invest just to raise enough seed money to buy the minimum equipment. Our business started catching fire quickly, and we made more money than we initially expected – 10 times our initial investment!

Our early success in the world of business inspired me to learn more. I began cold-emailing professors at multiple universities about research opportunities, and to my surprise, the Economics Department Chair at UNCC gave me a shot. Together, we researched sports economics, specifically addressing how sporting events impacted hotel revenues and small businesses in the Charlotte area over the last decade. This experience was eye-opening, as I not only learned how to run regression models, identify correlations through raw data, and write research papers, but I also witnessed the complexity of businesses and how vulnerable they can be to external factors.

My experience in business gives me confidence that I will enjoy business administration with a concentration in business analytics. At CMU, I look forward to sharing my past learnings and engaging in cutting-edge research. I will join finance and investment organizations like the Tepper Investment Club and leverage the university's strong industry connections to pursue meaningful internships. There's no doubt in my mind that CMU is the perfect place for me to further my love of business so that one day, I can own an impactful and meaningful business.

essays.prompt: Many students pursue college for a specific degree, career opportunity or personal goal. Whichever it may be, learning will be critical to achieve your ultimate goal. As you think ahead to the process of learning during your college years, how will you define a successful college experience? (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
A successful college experience isn't just about obtaining a degree; it's about using the skills and connections I have gained to harness the true power of technology to help various communities.

In the dynamic world of computer science, new frameworks and libraries are released by the day—literally. Hence, learning about these technologies is vital to growing as a programmer. Carnegie Mellon's environment will help me absorb and apply this knowledge to develop applications that serve a deeper purpose beyond fun projects.

Still, success extends beyond mastery of a particular framework. It requires the act of diversifying and building connections. At Carnegie Mellon, I plan to expand my network and spend time in this community, helping me broaden my understanding of concepts and fostering a sense of creativity. Establishing relationships with knowledgeable professors will also contribute to my success as they can provide valuable insights into technologies and their real-world applications. Success is not just individual achievement but rather collaborative innovation.

In this vibrant environment, I can add my own perspective to the university by establishing student organizations that help other engineers learn more about real-world development. Having won hackathons and other competitions, I can provide a unique stance, introducing a spirit of innovation and practicality into the academic landscape.

The ultimate goal is to leverage technology for the greater good. I hope to create a startup where I can develop innovative solutions to global issues. A successful experience at Carnegie Mellon will help me use my passion for computer science to reach this goal. This success is more than a destination; it's a journey that involves learning, collaboration, and innovation.

essays.prompt: Many students pursue college for a specific degree, career opportunity or personal goal. Whichever it may be, learning will be critical to achieve your ultimate goal. As you think ahead to the process of learning during your college years, how will you define a successful college experience? (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
In elementary school, we looked for special stamps on our tests. In middle school, it was a letter. In high school, it was a big jump up to numbers. Now, what's college? For 18 years, kids spend their time looking for one thing: academic validation.

To me, a successful college experience isn't getting good grades; it's the relationships you form and the conversations that actually change how you think.

In my 3 years of high school, I finally stopped seeing teachers as graders and started seeing them as people – people with stories, careers, and experiences I could actually learn from. The more I asked questions, the more I realized how much knowledge exists outside of the textbook. And that's exactly the type of learning I want to pursue in college.

At CMU, I want to take advantage of opportunities as simple as office hours or free time in class to develop a student-mentor relationship with my professors. I want to gain knowledge from their decades of experience instead of just learning how to solve a question. Hearing how they navigated their careers, how they approached failure, and how they think is far more valuable to me than checking off an assignment.

Communication is the foundation of business, and in college, it becomes the foundation of learning too. In competitive business fields, the difference between getting an opportunity and missing it often comes down to one thing: your network. By communicating with professors and peers, asking better questions, collaborating on ideas, and building genuine relationships, I'm practicing the exact skill that will help me break into those fields. College isn't just about getting straight A's; it's about learning to connect, and that ability will shape the trajectory of my career just as much as any class I take.

essays.prompt: Consider your application as a whole. What do you personally want to emphasize about your application for the admission committee's consideration? Highlight something that's important to you or something you haven't had a chance to share. Tell us, don't show us (no websites please). (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
I've never grown up with a lot of money. As a family, we've always had to be conscious of how we spend our money, and this has taught me frugality and financial wisdom. I've had to say no to friends and witness others face similar challenges. This fueled my determination to create a different reality—one where I have the wealth, not only to support myself but also to empower those I care about.

My pursuit of wealth is often misunderstood as a selfish and greedy desire. However, it isn't about building a luxury for myself—it stems from a deeper motivation for positive change. Money is an essential resource in today's world, and it is not possible to live without it. Money, to me, represents more than this personal comfort; it symbolizes the ability to support my loved ones and people in need.

My passion for computer science aligns with this pursuit for money. While I love to create new projects that require the use of advanced thinking and complex technologies, I also have to remember that programming is a tool to transcend financial constraints. My dream goes beyond programming—it's about utilizing my technological prowess to start a business that creates opportunities and products that benefit various communities across the globe.

When my business becomes successful, I may buy a fancy car or a nice house, but most of my earnings will go back to the people who helped me. My family, my friends, and my community. I can't, however, give back if I don't have any money, which is why I chase it. It's this mission to alleviate as much financial burden from others that motivates me to add one more line of code.

essays.prompt: Consider your application as a whole. What do you personally want to emphasize about your application for the admission committee's consideration? Highlight something that's important to you or something you haven't had a chance to share. Tell us, don't show us (no websites please). (300 word maximum)
essays.essay:
I want to emphasize my role as the Officer of Operations and Technology for the Charlotte Youth Marketing Association (CYMA).

From day one, we set out to position ourselves as a professional, student-led organization of entrepreneurs and marketers, not just another nonprofit. Our mission was simple but ambitious: to help local businesses expand their social footprint and grow their customer base through organic marketing.

We started by managing social media pages for small businesses across Charlotte. It wasn't easy to convince owners to trust a group of students, but through persistence with emails, calls, and face-to-face visits, we landed our first four clients. For them, we produced weekly content, designed flyers and managed promotional campaigns, which on average lifted revenue by 37% and reduced acquisition cost by 43%. In this process, we successfully taught owners how to use social media to reach new customers and build loyalty online.

CYMA eventually grew to more than 50 students, gaining hands-on experience in building content and networking. As our credibility and confidence grew, we took on larger projects, including hosting CYMA's first business showcase. For this event, we invited 20 local businesses and 13 organizations to promote themselves to over 150 attendees, making this an incredibly successful networking event. This solidified our reputation as a partner for businesses looking to scale.

What makes me proud isn't just the success of the event and the growth metrics, but the real value we delivered: giving business owners the tools to promote themselves, grow their customer base, and boost revenue without paying for advertising. Watching both the businesses we've touched and the members develop through CYMA showed me how much impact an organization can create when it knows its value. That's why I'm incredibly proud to be a part of CYMA.

essays.promptLabel: A time you disagreed with someone
essays.prompt: At Columbia, students representing a wide range of perspectives are invited to live and learn together. In such a community, questions and debates naturally arise. Please describe a time when you did not agree with someone and discuss how you engaged with them and what you took away from the interaction. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
One time when I did not agree with someone was when I was an intern at Global SVF. We were assigned the task of picking a nonprofit and writing a proposal so that the NPO can get investment. I wanted to invest in Youth Finance USA (YFUSA), while my peer wanted to invest in NFTE.

I suggested that we analyze both NPOs using our funds criteria, financial transparency, growth projection, and community reach. Through this discussion, we found that they were all at the same level for all the categories, except community reach, NFTE had a broader community impact. I realized that YFUSA aligned more with my passions, rather than the objective analysis. This experience taught me the value of separating personal bias from objective analysis, and how productive disagreement can lead to stronger, data-driven decisions, something I hope to continue practicing in Columbia's diverse and debate-driven community.

essays.prompt: In college/university, students are often challenged in ways that they could not predict or anticipate. It is important to us, therefore, to understand an applicant's ability to navigate through adversity. Please describe a barrier or obstacle you have faced and discuss the personal qualities, skills or insights you have developed as a result. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
Bella is my world. During the pandemic, she was an overweight border collie stuck in a critically unfunded adoption center in Korea after being rescued. The moment I saw her rotting toothy grin, and tongue-out eyes bulging, I knew she was going to be a part of my family. That's when I decided to take action.

Though my family was not easily convinced, they gave me the condition that if I involved myself with every step of the way, I would prove that I would be a worthy caretaker. And a worthy caretaker I became.

Paperwork, status updates, donations, I would dedicate six months to securing a home for her. Through this time, I had to lock in and focus on what was ahead. The process was not easy; managing stress on top of schoolwork made life difficult at points. But she's here now, and she's never going back.

essays.prompt: In college/university, students are often challenged in ways that they could not predict or anticipate. Please describe a barrier or obstacle you have faced and discuss the personal qualities, skills or insights you have developed as a result. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
At CYMA, we worked tirelessly to organize an event to help local businesses connect with attendees. One week before the event, the venue cancelled on us, and it sent the entire team into a scramble.

As Tech Lead, I had to switch gears quickly. I worked with my team to contact city officials about renting a public venue in my city and pitched the event to get the permit to use the space. We answered a flurry of questions about the logistics and negotiated the hours of operation, which enabled the officials to see how determined and prepared we were for this event. In the end, the event still had its hiccups, but it accomplished what we intended: to bring awareness to small businesses in the area. The experience changed how I approach challenges: instead of seeing obstacles as roadblocks, I now view them as opportunities to problem-solve and grow.

essays.prompt: A hallmark of the Columbia experience is being able to learn and thrive in an equitable and inclusive community with a wide range of perspectives. Tell us about an aspect of your own perspective, viewpoint or lived experience that is important to you, and describe how it has shaped the way you would learn from and contribute to Columbia's diverse and collaborative community. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
One lived experience that was important to who I am was teaching my first financial literacy workshop with 4H. Teaching them a topic as simple as budgeting helped snowball a journey towards investing and financial freedom. It helped me see how one lesson can start a kid's journey and help them achieve goals never thought of at such a young age.

This motivated me to start my own projects to get my foot in the door, and that start has led me to start businesses and complete projects I would never have thought of.

I want to help others in Columbia's community, get their foot in the door, and support them achieve their goals, even if I'm not physically doing the work. I believe that others in Columbia with that entrepreneurial spirit will also help me make that start that can open up endless opportunities that last a lifetime.

essays.prompt: A hallmark of the Columbia experience is being able to learn and thrive in an equitable and inclusive community with a wide range of perspectives. Tell us about an aspect of your own perspective, viewpoint or lived experience that is important to you, and describe how it has shaped the way you would learn from and contribute to Columbia's diverse and collaborative community. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
The color indigo is a heavily debated color. Should it be ROYGBIV or ROYGBV? Is it a shade of blue or purple? This may not be as significant as other burning disputes of the world, but the argument is of great value to me. It was the center of discussion between my friends over the years; this is my take.

I argue that this color should be highlighted. There must be a reason for it to belong in the rainbow. Whether it's more blue or purple, it's for the color itself to decide. What place are we in to conclude what it is?

It's just a color, yes. However, the concept is that it exists, just like the other hues of the visible rainbow. Similarly, Columbia University's varied community of perspectives, embracing and highlighting the different views is what makes the student body the most vivid group of beings seen.

essays.prompt: What attracts you to your preferred areas of study at Columbia College or Columbia Engineering? (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
What draws me to study Financial Economics at Columbia College is its emphasis on applying theory to real-world contexts. Specifically, ECON GU4230 (Economics of New York City) is a course that stands out because it connects the principles of economics to the city that surrounds it, turning New York into a living classroom.

While working with Professor Depken, I analyzed how sporting events influenced my city's hotel prices and how COVID reshaped spending patterns in this area. That experience showed me the power of location-focused economics and deepened my interest in how cities change and adapt.

At Columbia, I'm excited to continue exploring my curiosity through courses like this, where I can use real-world data to learn economics in a practical manner. Studying in New York is a dream and it would be amazing to learn more about the very place I'll be settling in for the next several years.

essays.prompt: Why are you interested in attending Columbia University? We encourage you to consider the aspect(s) that you find unique and compelling about Columbia. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
In all honesty, I had no idea what to do with myself until a year or two ago. The options of who I could become in the future distressed me, but it wasn't until I started to explore a variety of hobbies I concluded that I would be versatile with my future. With that I found myself standing before the digital stairs of Columbia University.

The wide range of diverse research opportunities around technology captured my interest, specifically the development of artificial intelligence impacting social life. With artificial intelligence constantly evolving, I questioned if it was possible to find solutions to the most critical of world issues. Columbia's Data Science Institute captures this very essence of expectations by providing the richest workshops, and collaborative opportunities and fostering the skills needed to meet these aspirations.

I hope to meet these values by climbing the steps of Columbia University.

essays.prompt: Why are you interested in attending Columbia University? We encourage you to consider the aspect(s) that you find unique and compelling about Columbia. (150 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
Columbia feels like the perfect blending of everything I love: the beautiful sunsets, the energy of a vibrant city, and being only a few steps from nature.

I can already imagine jogging through New York City, biking towards the Hudson to catch the orange sherbet sunsets as the day winds down. After class, I'd explore the city to find small food vendors that make New York so alive. And when I'm looking for something different, I'd stop by Max Soha for my favorite Italian comfort meals.

To me, Columbia isn't just a place to study. It's where I'll make happy memories and experience the heartbeat of the city I dreamed to live in. I'd push myself in school, but I'd also learn from New York itself – the culture, the economy, the street arts and more. This is exactly the type of environment that I want to be in.

essays.prompt: Why are you interested in the academic area(s) you indicated in your application? (Columbia supplemental; prompt not present in document, standard phrasing inferred.)
essays.essay:
It's 2:00 a.m., I should be sleeping, but I'm still wide awake, cruising the world through Google street view. When I can't tour the picturesque canals of Amsterdam or stylized streets of Mexico City in person, I find myself bundled under a blanket with an iPad and Google maps - my favorite way to relax.

With a Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African studies major at Columbia I hope to continue my travels, finding even more ways to infuse my global passion with discovery. Travelling the world has always been a part of my life, a gift and a privilege my parents have offered me, and I can't wait to reflect that in my studies.

Above all, I am an explorer, and at Columbia discovery is endless. My unbridled curiosity is what fuels my desire to travel the world, and in the future hopefully the vibrant streets of New York. The opportunity to learn across geographic borders and apply my experiences in an international major is incredibly exciting! Now if you'll excuse me, I've got more streets to explore.

essays.promptLabel: Texts and resources outside of academics
essays.prompt: List a selection of texts, resources and outlets that have contributed to your intellectual development outside of academic courses, including but not limited to books, journals, websites, podcasts, essays, plays, presentations, videos, museums and other content that you enjoy. (100 words or fewer)
essays.essay:
Watching Esports has been a guilty pleasure of mine for the longest time. It wasn't the competitive scene of video games that drew me in, but the analysis behind the most impressive plays.

Rewatching old tournaments and breaking down every movement of winners inspired me to apply similar skills to the real world. Through practices of scanning strategies, I refined my abilities to study texts, manage my time, and find the most efficient ways to solve problems. It may not be seen as an academic source in society, but the competitive gaming environment impacted the way I view MY academics.

essays.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others.
essays.essay:
I wrote my first book in the second grade.

It involved diagonal stick-figures and triangle shaped trees, illegible squiggles that were supposed to depict words, and only five pages long. To save you the trouble of reading it, although it's completely illegible, my main character Suzy was able to fight off the dragon and reach her happy ending in a matter of five pages. Five. Pages.

It was too easy, but then again I was seven years old. All I knew was easy.

I was a manic child, running from play structure to play structure. My legs moved faster than my mind could keep up the majority of the time. Yet, I was never afraid of my knee getting scraped or elbow bruised, because I knew that my mom would always be there to massage in some Neosporin and wrap my battle wound in a Hello Kitty bandaid every time. Even in the third grade, this kid would scribble all over a drawing of mine I poured my heart into and before I even let the hot tears escape the teacher was already scolding him.

Unfortunately, things didn't stay easy forever. And I grew up.

I became obsessed with Harry Potter, as every thirteen year old is. And I wanted to write my own "chosen one" story. So, I started to write. It had witches and vampires and werewolves, but I only got one chapter in before I decided that I wasn't cut out to write something so intense, regardless of how much I wanted to. I decided that I should start smaller, but at the time even that felt too hard. Writing as a hobby started to get complicated for me.

I definitely changed, but I didn't know if I liked who I became. For me, it was a time of firsts.

I received my first bad grade and I couldn't decide if I should drop out or pretend I didn't care. I went to my first school dance and awkwardly clung to the wall. I got my first boyfriend and we held hands, said things we didn't mean, walked each other to class, until he dumped me over text a month later. I had my first fight with my mom and trust me, it didn't go over well.

At the end of that crazy rollercoaster, thankfully, I got older.

J.D. Salinger became my literary idol, even though I could barely understand anything he said without looking it up. I matured. I became committed to writing something that meant something to someone. No witches. No vampires. No werewolves. It took multiple attempts until I was able to succeed a year later. I contemplated giving up more times than I'm proud to admit, to toss it in the "never going to finish" pile and leave it there to rot, but the passion I had for writing prevailed and is what ultimately kept me going. And I'm proud of myself for that, for being able to come to the keyboard to type word after word even when it felt like it wouldn't amount to anything.

I was pleasantly surprised, because my junior year of high school I self-published my first novel.

Time was my ultimate wingman, because it gave me the chance to be a person that I'd gladly identify being. I discovered that even if I dress different from the norm, it's something to take pride in. I experienced friends coming and going all throughout high school, but I know that it was probably for the best and I wish them well. I finally accepted that there will always be bad mixed in with the good, but the world is full of successes, you just have to acknowledge them and celebrate!

Over the years I've grown as a writer, but more importantly as an individual.

And as the world around me broadens, I can't wait to grow some more.

essays.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?
essays.essay:
Entrepreneurship always looks easy on social media. Teens earning thousands from side hustles over platforms like Instagram and Tiktok, making it seem like starting a business is risk-free. I wanted to try this myself, so my friend and I started a car detailing business with the goal of replicating the success we see online. It didn't take long before our business hit a major barrier: getting leads and making sales.

Deciding on a car detailing business came as second nature for my friend and I. We loved cars and wanted to invest in a business where our seed money would go towards a business that we felt passionate about and accountable for. Car detailing is a business that fits this profile perfectly – no shortcuts and a lot of physical, but rewarding, work. We also wanted a service business model where there is genuine human interaction rather than selling a product in a digital shopping cart because it would teach us to be better negotiators and help us build more confidence in selling.

It started well. We invested our initial dollars into cleaning products and practiced on our parents' cars which ended up as clean as a freshly polished steel pan right out of the box. We did door-to-door sales, selling our services to neighbors and then took our confidence to a local Facebook group where our first post generated a few happy customers. We felt the rush of a small business teeming with life, only to realize a few short weeks after that we didn't have returning customers to support our growth. Our revenue evaporated like water on a hot hood, and there we were, sitting hopeless and clueless. What do we do next? So this is what "churn" feels like in business. We felt gutted because what looked like a promising start with more than satisfied customers turned south so quickly, and we didn't have any answers to this problem.

Then, one night, while scrolling through the app that sold us his feverish business dream (TikTok), we stumbled across a video promoting a local car show. Instantly, something clicked. It was a momentary thought, but what if we showed up at a car show with our services? What if we were knocking on the wrong doors. At a car show, these are enthusiasts that probably washed their cars more than their dishes, and if we could provide them with top-notch detailing services, it would solve a problem they never knew they had.

That weekend, we drove to a "Cars and Coffee" event with a box of freshly printed business cards. We were nervous, but we were too deeply invested in this business to let it fail. At the car show, we sold our hearts out, but more importantly, we listened. We listened to the car owners' pains and groans when it came to keeping their cars clean and we opened our pockets as they poured in advice about how we can grow our business through car shows. We ended up booking a few appointments on the spot and by the following week, we were fully booked. Since then, our business has grown to one of the largest car detailing services in my city, making around 50 sales a month.

That car show didn't just revive our business, it reshaped how I perceive challenges. We didn't need better products, or flashier branding; we needed to listen and observe. This experience showed me that sometimes, the best action is by staying put, absorbing information and making careful decisions. Even more important is that I learned how to pivot; taking a left turn in decision making when I need to. Sometimes, I tend to fight the feeling of change and I get complacent with moving in the same direction even if it means digging myself a deeper hole, but learning to pivot has really helped me in business and in school.

essays.prompt: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?
essays.essay:
In front of me, the word "Defeat" printed onto my screen. The dark, gloomy text reflected my pouty expression - I hated that word. However, the irritation soon depleted and I embarked on my next adventure into the next game. Never once have I felt pressured, stressed or even frustrated with playing games. Like my fictional virtual avatar, I flapped my wings and I took off, free and happy.

However, things took a turn when I met one of my first internet friends. At first, I assumed she was just someone who needed a friend to play with. Little did I know, opening up to her would transform me in ways I never would have imagined. We'd talk hours on end about life simultaneously to playing video games, there would never be a dull moment, I thought. It looked as if I had found my other half, my best friend. I thought I had it all, I thought I was free.

But something loomed over me, a gut feeling stirred and I never seemed to pick up those feelings until it was too late. I found myself enjoying video games less and less, why do I get so irrationally upset when things go wrong? Where was this coming from?

Then it all clicked, but it clicked all too late. The person I relied on, I spent 3 years talking everyday to, who made me feel like I had it all, was molding me into her ideal person. Whenever I didn't do what she wanted to do, I was bombarded with guilt tripping messages like "You always misunderstand me. You never listen." If I played games with my friends, I was faced with "Oh ok. That's fine." or "Ok whatever just replace me I guess." Each and every hateful message I received, a blade cut deeper and deeper into my already aching heart. But for some reason, I left what was hurting me the most lodged deep in the core of me.

I took matters into my own hands when I was confronted with the offense for the very last time. With a single button, I removed her from my life and I was left there with what felt like nothing. My grades were low and I was detached from my friends. Even my once comforting video games seemed like a distant realm rather than home.

Did I waste my opportunities? Did I waste my time?

Fortunately, I found my thoughts to be completely, utterly wrong. The first goal I set for myself was to get my head back into school. As soon as I got home from school, my head was in the books. The grades that were once buried away, sprung up with A's and high B's. A wave of accomplishment swept me away and wrapped its arms around me. My wings that were once clipped by unfortunate events, healed and granted me to soar once again. I was on air. I know I am capable of great resilience, I have opportunity.

The once distant relationships I had with my friends soon disappeared when I reached out to them. I was met with the warm comfort of their presence once again. In addition to my healing bonds, I slowly brought video games back into my life. The once stressful, suffocating environment was lifted and they became a medium of creativity and exploration.

From a young carefree gamer, to a resilient individual finding myself in the trenches of emotions I learned that embracing the uncertainties will not only keep me on my feet, but let me rekindle passions and redefine my relationship with myself. I've taken back my life into my own hands, and found a strength that'll carry me through challenges. In video games, encountering challenges means that you are going in the right direction. In the end, I turned my series of defeats into my proudest victory.

essays.prompt: The Common Application personal statement (prompt not specified in source; topic of the student's choice).
essays.essay:
You may not be able to judge a book by its cover, but you can learn a lot about someone from their shoes. At 12 years old, I bought and resold shoes. At 7:00 am sharp, I'd rush to "cop" a coveted sneaker and by 7:01 they'd be sold out. While I always viewed these shoes as just a vehicle for investment, the immense demand for these sneakers made me think: there must be more to shoes than meets the eye.

After years of visiting, a quaint Dutch town where my oma and opa (grandparents) lived has become my second home. With its venerable castles, cheery cafes, and small-town spirit, it is a place I know by heart. One day, while adventuring around town, I heard the distinct sound of a group of men in klompen - the traditional wooden shoes of the Netherlands. My curiosity must have been obvious because a kind old man within the group noticed my fascination, took off his klompen, and pointed to me to try them on. I didn't hesitate. While rigid at first, they were surprisingly comfortable and fun to wear. The "clickety-clock" beneath my feet and the signature cobalt blue and yellow dyes fascinated me to no end. I would come to realize that the klompen were more than just footwear – they reflected Dutch culture and more importantly, my heritage – practical, structured, and straightforward, yet colorful and cheerful. Above all, the hard yet vibrant klompen mirrors a valuable part of who I am, someone that embraces tradition and structure while exuding an unlimited sense of positivity and joy.

If this town is my second home, Istanbul is equally my third. While helping clean my aneaneane's (grandmother) apartment, I discovered a pair of charik, a traditional Turkish shoe made of leather that dates back to the Hittites in 1300 BCE near my mother's birthplace. Just as the leather hugs the foot, Turkish culture embraces everyone with open arms. Here, friends and family are abundant and connections are deep and spontaneous. Neighbors knock late at night to share a plate of food, friends stop by for unexpected Turkish coffee and fortune-telling – there is simply no better representation of hospitality than living in a Turkish family.

One of these unplanned connections after another led me to meet a group of primary school kids in the Eastern part of Turkey, near the Syrian border. I taught English virtually to these kids and hoped to share with them the broadness of the world and its possibilities. The first time I turned on the video to teach, the kids gathered together, eyes wide and grinning with excitement. In the background were bare walls, and I noticed their shoes - worn, old, dusty and a little torn. Their shoes told a story that needed no words, and I instinctively made sure to keep my shoes out of sight. Over many sessions, we bonded. I became "Abi" (big brother), a title I'll always hold close to heart. In a way, the charik are a fitting symbol of Turkish culture and what this experience has taught me: flexibility, resilience, and the beauty of forming connections, no matter the circumstances or distance. Turkish culture has taught me to embrace everyone, to care for others, and to give without expecting anything in return.

Back at home, I carry these experiences — and shoes – with me. These days, when I'm not admiring the shoes others are wearing and imagining what it says about them, I'm mindful of the ones I wear. I believe there isn't one shoe that does it all. Likewise, there isn't only one way to approach the challenges and gifts that life has to offer. That's why I wear a different shoe for all the different occasions in my life, much like how I adapt to the myriad of challenges that come my way: one shoe at a time.

essays.promptLabel: Finding balance amid a parent's illness
essays.prompt: Personal statement (topic of your choice) — a Common Application main essay. [Prompt not stated in source; inferred.]
essays.essay:
Living just 10 minutes from the coastline, I found solace at the beach near my home. The sound of the waves, the occasional sunset, and the endless horizon served as a haven from the unpredictable pace of my life. But everything changed in February of 2021 as my family was driving on the highway along the coast. A new wave came crashing in, one I never saw coming: my mom was diagnosed with stage 2 lymphoma in her liver.

In the first few weeks following her diagnosis, I buried myself in schoolwork and chores, filling the silence with podcasts or music to block out the helplessness. I came to believe that if I could stay busy enough, I could regain control in this chaos. Yet I failed to recognize the walls I had put up with my family and friends. At school, I kept my headphones in, avoiding conversations. At home, the looks on my parents' faces after every long day were a constant reminder that nothing I had done could help this situation. Fearing the idea of having to explain my emotions, my grasp was slowly eroding the relationships I was trying to hold onto.

One evening, during another agonizingly quiet dinner centered around our screens, I made unintentional eye contact with my dad. His eyes were glistening off the dining room light and I could see the fragility brimming out of them. It was the first time I didn't look away. I didn't avoid it. Silence enveloped the air, but this time, I allowed myself to sit with it instead of filling it with noise or distraction. In all of my frantic attempts to manage everything in my life, I misunderstood what I needed most: balance—understanding that these unexpected factors didn't need to be controlled or avoided. They needed to be acknowledged.

And so, I began to loosen my grip, allowing raw conversations to seep into my life. I made an effort to become more transparent during dinners, often asking for updates and creating a space where we could thrive in honesty. I assured them that if something came up, I would be ready to take on a couple more responsibilities around the house. However, I also came to see that without the need for distractions, the mutual presence of one another was enough to ease the anxiety within us. Instead of trying to fix the unfixable, showing up, understanding, and holding space for uncertainty proved to be the most invaluable. With friends, the less I bound myself to my headphones, the more I started to understand how nurturing the act of presence was. During one of their especially complicated breakups, instead of offering advice, I just sat with her. I listened—no filling silence or coming up with quick fixes. In return, she offered space where I was able to share how I was feeling. Simply being present meant more than any piece of advice I could've ever given.

I started to embrace this new perspective, and I found it spilling into other areas of my life. I became more genuine with the connections I made, learning to appreciate the quiet understanding that can pass between two people without words. I extended this to those in my community as well, starting a chapter of a charity organization at my school that bridged the gap between seniors and youth within my city through hand-made cards. Whether it was helping individuals find meaning in having these conversations or providing an outlet to do so, I saw how the simple act of understanding could build deep connections.

Now, as I take a stroll on that same beach, feeling the steady rhythm of the waves is a warming reminder of the balance I've found. No longer encased by fear or control, I can truly embrace the calm and the connection in the waters around me, surrounded by those I've grown to build everlasting relationships with.

essays.prompt: Personal statement (topic of your choice) — describe who you are through your interests, experiences, and passions. [Prompt not stated in source; inferred.]
essays.essay:
My life is a pallet of colorful experiences that have shaped me into the adaptable, passionate, and always enthusiastic learner that I am today. I have a sizable appetite for trying new things - be it thrilling experiences like skydiving at Yosemite and hot air ballooning in the Napa Valley or self-indulging activities like mud bathing in Calistoga and attending paint night events at local coffee shops. And although reluctantly supportive at times - and understandably so - my parents have always provided me with the resources to help add to the vibrant lifestyle that I lead.

On the flipside is an academic driven version of myself. When it's time to put down the skydiving equipment and align my vision towards my studies, I make it a priority to commit to the field of psychology and neuroscience by engaging in cutting edge research. That's why in the summer of 2018, I interned with the Community Psychology Team at the University of California, Santa Cruz to research the effects of social empowerment in Latinx children. This experiment was both taxing and gratifying. I spent hours each week documenting and assessing data on spreads and charts, but found joy in being able to interact with and learn from a group of bright minded children. I remember feeling attached to the children that I worked with; the connection we made in the process of learning about each other was genuinely important to me. And for the first time, I felt comfortable working under the pressure of my responsibilities.

In 2019, I returned to the university with greater ambitions to study the biological side of psychology: neuroscience. This was a major stepping stone for me to become involved in the medical field. On my first day, I recall feelings of elation and anxiousness while studying the laboratory protocols. I was taken back to the early days of high school science experiments, only this time I was paired with PhD candidates and post-docs that were determined to tap into the ground-breaking research of neural stem cell differentiation and its implications of ALS and autism. The work involved was pioneering, with the potential to help hundreds of existing and future patients. I was prepared to put in my fair share of work to contribute to the advancement of medicine. My responsibilities were not light and varied each day - from sectioning mice brains into precise patterns and combing through volumes of cryptic numbers to performing gel electrophoresis and polymerase chain reactions (PCR). This kept me keen and perpetually fascinated as the lab results were oftentimes unexpected and convoluted. This was also the first time that I saw the concepts and biological engineering practices come to life; it was stimulating and insightful.

Outside of the lab, I change out of my lab coat and enjoy a different lifestyle. I don't believe that life is all about textbooks and reaching for academic milestones, but it's easy to get lost in an academic rabbit hole with the status quo of education being built around competition. Instead, I often identify with activities outside of academia to give my mind the rest it needs to stay sharp and focused. I feel most comfortable when I am out in the woods setting up a tripod for the perfect photograph to add to my growing portfolio or when I am at the beach soaking in my weekly dose of sunlight. It's such a therapeutic sensation to be connected to the outdoors and it is this mentality that keeps me healthy all around. But apart from my love of the outdoors, I spent the last 8 years practicing classical Indian dance and have been honored as one of the youngest students in the world to receive a Bachelors of Dance (Bharatanatyam) from the Art Society of Mumbai. To date, this is my proudest accomplishment. Dance is not only a part of my heritage, but it is an exquisite form of self-expression and a rich form of cultural narrative.

essays.prompt: Personal statement (topic of your choice) — a Common Application main essay. [Prompt not stated in source; inferred.]
essays.essay:
I've developed the perfect technique for peeling an orange.

Using a knife, make a forty-five-degree incision near the top of the fruit. It's a technique I taught myself in February of 2021 when my family received a menacing call. My mom had been diagnosed with stage 2 lymphoma in her liver, and suddenly, I found myself backed into a corner I didn't recognize. The bubble of constant security I had always found in my parents' presence had burst. The first slight cut into the orange marked my initial steps away from the comfort of that bubble.

Score the skin. Make four shallow vertical cuts from top to bottom, following the natural curve of the fruit. For the majority of my life, I had relied on my parents to shoulder much of the family responsibilities. Coming home and knowing that there would be a plate of fruit waiting for me felt like a comforting routine. But as new cuts made their way into the orange, that sense of convenience also faded. With their schedules completely booked with radiation therapy sessions and endless nights Googling medical terms, I had to manage things on my own. This new responsibility was like a pit in my stomach, and it often felt overwhelming. There were countless nights when I hovered over a tissue box, longing for times before my bubble had burst. Whatever doubt remained would be quickly dismissed though, as I knew I had no choice but to continue. For my parents, for all the things I could no longer ignore or push off, and for me.

With your thumb, begin to peel the skin off the orange, layer by layer. This orange's skin was particularly thick, a reminder of just how deeply rooted my reliance on my parents had been. Nevertheless, day after day, I cut and peeled, the rinds piling high in the compost bin. At first, every approach I tried was unsuccessful. The cuts would be jagged and uneven. The peel would tear at awkward times, and I would become frustrated with myself. But slowly, my technique began to shift and develop. I found that a good knife grip and using just the right amount of pressure would make better cuts. In turn, the peel could be removed more smoothly. I began to notice this shift within myself as well, feeling less doubtful and more optimistic each day. I was learning to carve out a life that wasn't defined by another's effort but by my own. Beneath all these layers of orange rinds, I discovered something that I had come to overlook: my potential. The orange that had once been protected by its outer peel was now exposed for what it truly was. Similarly, I was slowly learning about this version of myself that could thrive without needing to live inside a bubble.

Separate the orange into halves, then into slices. Every orange I peeled served as a stepping stone that only made me more confident in my ability to tackle the next unexpected challenge. Now, every time I finish peeling the four bowls of oranges, I feel proud and content. It is not because my technique is on par with that of Gordon Ramsay's cutting skills, but because I had done it, and that was what mattered the most. No longer am I a girl who relies on her parents to solve every problem for her. I am now a girl who can face those problems by myself. Peeling oranges has shown me that you do not gain independence overnight, but rather earn it, often by overcoming unfamiliarity and persevering through it. With the outer peel removed, what remains is sweeter, and by shedding my dependence, I now allow independence to seep into every corner of my life.

Next time, I'll show you how to cut an apple.

essays.prompt: Some students have a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it. If this sounds like you, then please share your story.
essays.essay:
Knock, knock.

“Can my friend come out?” “Can my other friend come outside?”

That was me, every single day for five years in what I call my serial-door knocker phase. At 4PM sharp, I become the neighborhood alarm clock, buzzing door-to-door like a salesman giving my best pitch to parents who could already recite my lines. There were seven of us in our close circle and we had all met in the community park where we shared the field, the courts, and the playground.

By 4:15, roll call was complete. We laced up, grabbed our gear and raced towards the park. We weren't all too creative like some of the other children who seemed to invent new games every other day. For us, it was either soccer, cricket, or chess.

For me, soccer was by far my favorite. Every kid's soccer journey starts off with a vital decision: Messi or Ronaldo. I was Messi on the field, imitating his sequences and movements that were etched in my memory. Everyday, we'd try something different on the field. Some days a crossbar challenge where we'd compete on accuracy by trying to hit the metal frame on the goal; other days we'd scrimmage, helping each other train to compete against other teams. Years on the field with this group taught me the value of friendship and the power of team spirit. Together, we also developed a competitive mentality, always playfully taunting each other to one-up another, and this competitiveness became a powerful force in school where I always challenged myself without hesitation.

When our soccer cleats were retired for the week, we'd move on to play cricket. Cricket always brought a crowd on the sidelines as kids and adults competed on the makeshift field that wasn't really suitable for the sport. Even when I wasn't playing, I'd share a picnic mat with my family as we cheered on the players. This is what made cricket really special: it made me feel connected to my family and my community, and as a child, this feeling of unity was tremendously impactful in shaping my values. Each time I play cricket, and see all the wonderful families celebrating our efforts, I'm reminded that I have a huge support system and I owe it to my parents for giving me this upbringing.

Beyond the physical conditioning of cricket, the years spent on the field have strengthened my strategic thinking and helped me stay calm under pressure. There were a number of memorable tie-breaker games where we had to coordinate creative plays and experiment with new batting techniques. And while we still lost a few matches, we were incredibly happy to have just survived such a high-endurance game. Yet again, this composure carried into other parts of my life, both in school and in how I communicate, always staying level-headed amidst adversity.

Off the green, chess was a game we were passionate about. In third grade, my dad taught me to maneuver the board, memorizing classic moves used by Kasparov. I excelled in classic chess and competed in online tournaments which often lasted weeks. I shared this love of chess with my friends, and the seven of us would rotate at each other's houses to compete for the highest rank. Eventually, we discovered blitz chess, a sped-up version of the game where I witnessed the importance of decisiveness and reactivity – both of which are elements of adaptability. Playing chess with the boys was more than just weekend shenanigans, it was a time where we all trained our minds to be tactical and sharp.

The times we shared together truly dictated the person I am today. We built inseparable friendships that a change of zip code would have no effect on; and in fact, my family did move across the country, but nothing has changed. The lessons, laughter, and bond we built still guide me every day.

All of these “phases” allowed us to grow one way or another, whether it was athletically, technically, or thoughtfully. They helped us build inseparable friendships with competition that drove us to greatness. Eventually however, life happened and we all started moving to houses, or across the country. But one thing I do know is that without these phases all of us would be completely different people, and these core phases helped us become well rounded individuals ready to take on any obstacle. That's why I believe these phases are so meaningful to me, these phases are who I am.

essays.prompt: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked a period of personal growth and a new understanding of yourself or others. [Prompt not explicitly stated; the applicant's notes referenced Common App prompts #7/#3.]
essays.essay:
In early 2020, a small, fragile plant found its place atop my album-filled shelf. Bearing a mere two leaves and a peculiarly thin stem, its fragile nature was something I put much of my focus on in a time where I was confined to my room. Each day blended into the next and caring for the plant became one of a few purposeful activities. Despite my good intentions, I had no idea how to take care of it.

How often was I supposed to water it? Once a day? Once a week? Maybe every two weeks? My impatience led me to water it daily, eager for any sign of growth, any sign that I was doing it right. Much to my dismay, the bigger of the two leaves turned yellow a week after I watered it. A month later, my first plant died—overwatered, something I learned only after I attempted to take it off the top of my shelf, when a flood of excess water spilled down my shirt.

Learning from my first plant, I paid attention to the frequency of my watering with my second, more sizable one. Instead of watering it everyday, I watered it every three days, a pattern I discovered after checking the moisture level of the dirt. Riddled with anticipation, I waited for the plant to show signs of growth, only to be once again stumped as multiple leaves started turning brown. Upon further research, I realized that I had placed the plant in an area with too much sunlight concentration. Moving the plant three inches to the left solved that problem.

As my top shelf slowly grew into a forest, I began to notice the subtle differences between each plant. I began to understand that growth wasn't defined by quickness or overambitious attempts to speed up a process. Each plant had its own unique set of needs—some thrived in direct sunlight, others preferred the shade; some required more water, others less. I learned how to listen and respond, observing the small details that revealed what was needed for each plant to thrive.

This newfound awareness wasn't limited to just my plants—it started to shape how I approached other areas of my life. As I delved deeper into medicine, I began to see similar patterns. Each clinical experience, whether working with patients or collaborating with staff, added another layer of understanding to my approach. While working at the pediatric clinic, I quickly realized that open appointment slots after 3:00PM should be offered to patients who were still in school since it usually ended around that time. On the other hand, the optometry clinic usually offered early weekend appointments as patients may have plans in the latter half of the day. Both internships used two different systems and I had to acclimate to both.

These patterns weren't observed immediately though. I made some mistakes in the beginning as I was rushing, trying to take on too much at once. However, with every new experience, I learned to pace myself. I became more aware of the nuances of time, communication, and patient care, understanding that what worked in one situation might not work in another.

Much like my plants, I began to realize that growth in medicine didn't happen overnight. It came from consistently showing up, learning from each encounter, and adjusting my approach with each new challenge. Just as I'd carefully assess the needs of each plant, I started to appreciate the processes of the medical field—the way each patient, each environment required its own kind of attention. It was through these learning experiences where I learned how to water my knowledge, give it the right amount of light, and allow it to grow naturally, trusting that, with patience, the expertise I sought would begin to emerge.

essays.prompt: The Common Application personal statement (prompt not specified in source; reflects on personal growth through the student's photography passion).
essays.essay:
Want to step up your photography game and set yourself apart from the other "generic" photographers? I'll tell you how!

Could it be the lighting and how light smoothly cascades into a shadow, giving your subject a soft, desirable appearance? Could it be good image composition? Oh! Could it be that your subject looks beautiful?

Well, not really…

I discovered my passion for photography during a counseling meeting with my sophomore counselor. Since then, I have been wrestling with the answer to the question: what makes a great photo? Well, although I do not have a clear answer, after three years of studying photography and running my own photography business, here is what I've discovered so far.

Tip #1: Make the best of the light you have.

Lighting doesn't have to be perfect. You don't need a studio with three large lights fully equipped with diffusers and grids. Sometimes, the best photos are taken when the situations are not ideal. It has been difficult for me to break the habit of canceling photoshoots due to lousy weather, similar to how it's been challenging to break other bad habits such as avoiding social interactions and excessively spending money. However, the funny thing is, some of the best photos I've taken were in conditions where the lighting was unideal. Whether it's in harsh sunlight, which amplifies the imperfections of a subject's face, or in the pouring rain, the "unidealness" of the light gives my photos a unique, authentic feel. I have embraced unideal light, just as I have embraced unideal life situations. For example, my family is far from perfect. Still, it is moments when we experience darkness, such as when my mother contracted COVID-19, that allow us to focus on the light we have and unite as one.

Tip #2: Take risks with new styles.

Second, your photo doesn't have to be perfectly composed. The subject doesn't need to be in a flawless position with the best camera angle and perfectly in focus. Sometimes, professional photographers deliberately put their subjects out of focus. Others take their photos on multi-thousand dollar cameras and edit them to look like they were taken by a cheap Polaroid camera. Taking amazing photos, I've realized, means taking risks and breaking from the norm. This could mean trying new, bold color palettes or opening your shutter for a longer time to capture dynamic movement in your photo. This willingness to take risks has permeated into my high school experience, as I have stepped out of my comfort zone and taken leadership roles such as becoming an Executive Student Council member and the President of the Christian Service and Justice Club.

Tip 3: Capture goodness.

Lastly, your subject doesn't have to follow conventional beauty standards. I believe that the best photos aren't the ones that look the best, but they are the ones that speak the best. The best example I have is the photo documentation book by Michael Collopy, Works of Love are Works of Peace. In the book, stark images of the sick, the handicapped, and the outcasts of society are shown receiving care from volunteers. The photos are heartbreaking, but they are beautiful. The images are black and white, and yet full of color. These photos go beyond just looking good on the surface - they go deeper and express the goodness of humanity. In the future, I want to engage in activities that lift others up, and I'm determined to find a path that will allow me to grow so that I can serve others positively.

Therefore, if there is a piece of advice that I can leave you with today so that you may take great photos, I'd say, "Be a good person, bring your camera with you as you do good things, and don't let norms or unideal light get in your way."

Oh, and learning how to use a camera helps too.

essays.prompt: Common Application main personal statement (topic of your choice). [Inferred: the document labels this section "Common App Front Page."]
essays.essay:
My life is a palette of colorful experiences that have shaped me into the adaptable, passionate, and always enthusiastic learner that I am today. I have a sizeable appetite for trying new things - be it thrilling experiences like skydiving at Yosemite and hot air ballooning in the Napa Valley or self-indulging activities like mud bathing in Calistoga and attending paint night events at local coffee shops. And although reluctantly supportive at times - and understandably so - my parents have always provided me with the resources to help add to the vibrant lifestyle that I lead.

On the flipside is an academic driven version of myself. When it's time to put down the skydiving equipment and align my vision towards my studies, I make it a priority to commit to the field of psychology and neuroscience by engaging in cutting edge research. That's why in the summer of 2018, I interned with the Community Psychology Team at the University of California, Santa Cruz to research the effects of social empowerment in Latinx children. This experiment was both taxing and gratifying. I spent hours each week documenting and assessing data on spreads and charts, but found joy from interacting with and learning from a group of bright minded children. I remember feeling attached to the children that I worked with; the connection we made in the process of learning about each other was genuinely important to me. And for the first time, I felt comfortable working under the pressure of my responsibilities.

In 2019, I returned to the university with greater ambitions to study the biological side of psychology: neuroscience. This was a major stepping stone for me to become involved in the medical field. On my first day, I recall feelings of elation and anxiousness while studying the laboratory protocols. I was taken back to the early days of high school science experiments, only this time I was paired with PhD candidates and post-docs that were determined to tap into the ground-breaking research of neural stem cell differentiation and its implications of ALS and autism. The work involved was pioneering, with the potential to help thousands of existing and future patients, and I was prepared to contribute to the advancement of medicine. My responsibilities were not light and varied each day - from sectioning mice brains into precise patterns and combing through volumes of cryptic numbers to performing gel electrophoresis and polymerase chain reactions (PCR). This kept me keen and perpetually fascinated as the lab results were often times unexpected and convoluted. This was also the first time that I saw the concepts and biological engineering practices come to life; it was stimulating and insightful.

Outside of the lab, I change out of my lab coat and enjoy a different lifestyle. I don't believe that life is all about textbooks and reaching for academic milestones, but it's easy to get lost in an academic rabbit hole with the status quo of education being built around competition.
