essays.promptLabel: Beliefs challenged by another point of view
essays.prompt: USC believes that one learns best when interacting with people of different backgrounds, experiences and perspectives. Tell us about a time you were exposed to a new idea or when your beliefs were challenged by another point of view. (250 words)
essays.essay:
Growing up in a state with an ever-shifting political climate, I've always been aware of many debates and public outcries that seem to divide the Californian population.

Some years ago, I felt like I had been on the backseat of every political discussion - which isn't too out of norm because I was in my early teens and every discourse were limited within classroom set-ups. Now that I'm well within maturation, I've been finding myself more readily engaged on serious topics such as changes in state policies.

One good instance of this was how, as a child, I've always been in opposition with all types of "vices", mostly just parroting the views of my elders. These beliefs were immediately challenged during the summer of 2018 when I started doing community service in a Veterans Affairs hospital.

There, the basic tasks included providing assistance to veteran patients, assisting them on how to use technology and readjust to society. We've monitored their prescribed medication and saw which treatments worked with patients who were going through severe PTSD. With most of the former pills not working, we saw how easier access to cannabinoids such as Marinol helped our veterans regain their appetite and, in certain ways, their will to live.

After seeing a lot of patients respond more positively with the new prescriptions, I realized these findings surpassed the sort of moral dilemmas we once held, and that we could push for better treatment options without having to resort into anything prejudicial.

essays.prompt: The student body at the USC Viterbi School of Engineering is a diverse group of unique engineers and computer scientists who work together to engineer a better world for all humanity. Describe how your contributions to the USC Viterbi student body may be distinct from others.
essays.essay:
Coming from an Asian family in California where my parents were first-generation immigrants, I've learned to appreciate the rich traditions of my heritage while being open-minded to the innovative spirit of Silicon Valley. Teaching young kids in math and arts has not only provided me great satisfaction from helping others but also deepened my appreciation for teachers. It has also instilled in me patience and empathy that I believe are important not only in collaborating with others but also in building a better world for humanity.

Moreover, my experiences with LGBT groups and friends have broadened my perspectives and cultivated a deep respect for diversity and inclusivity. I believe that an environment where all voices are heard and valued will create a better world.

I am excited to join the USC Viterbi student body, who are not just solving problems together but are also dedicated to making the world a more understanding and peaceful place for humanity.

essays.promptLabel: Experiences/skills for World Bachelor in Business
essays.prompt: What experiences and/or skills best prepare you for success in our World Bachelor in Business program? (250 words)
essays.essay:
My vocabulary began as a mixed string of Turkish and Dutch words. Over time, my ability to speak English has grown, but I still carry that same connection with my lineage. In all, I have travelled to Turkey 14 times, and the Netherlands 12 times. They are my homes away from home, and I couldn’t imagine life without them.

Yet, despite my experience visiting abroad, I know that I have so much to learn. In fact, the more I travel the larger the Earth feels, and I can’t imagine how much more experiences I have yet to seek out in WBB. That being said, to handle spontaneous moments in travelling when plans need to be changed, I have learned to take action without looking back. When a devastating 7.8 magnitude earthquake struck the Turkish/Syrian border, I was determined to do my part to help. Working with my school, I organized a fundraiser and raised $2,200. When mental health issues soared after the pandemic, I had to be creative to find a solution. Experimenting with landscape chippers and eventually collaborating with another nonprofit, I was able to convert used tennis balls into squishy stress relievers. Finally, when I was in Turkey and an Impactful Tennis coach left for Texas on a whim, I had to suddenly reschedule 19 lessons.

While no one experience can prepare me for college traveling abroad, I know that my background and ability to act will help me take the first step forward.

essays.prompt: Acknowledging that the WBB does not offer a "traditional" or fixed residential experience, please explain why this alternative education experience is a good fit for you. Please share examples of how you plan to create unique or new opportunities in the WBB environment. (250 words)
essays.essay:
Some people want to travel, experience new cultures and meet people from different backgrounds. I am one of them. Maybe the interest in different parts of the world was implanted in me through my parents and their background, or maybe it was my grandmother who passed on her love of archeology, history and art to us over the years little by little through stories. Regardless, I love tasting different foods, learning about different cultures, and meeting people from other places. This year I wanted to fulfill that interest by convincing my parents to lend me some of their accumulated mileage for a trip to Japan that I fully organized. I traveled to different Japanese cities via the train system I so admire and experienced a little part of the culture. Given my interests combined with my desire to study business, I believe the WBB program is the perfect fit for me with the opportunity to study in three global locations and create global business impact.

I will in turn share my cultural experiences and learnings through working and studying in the US and Turkey. I will schedule learning sessions, do orientations on how to adapt to working in a different place than where you grew up based on my experience. I would also serve as a guide to anyone who wants to learn about European impact projects that help underdeveloped countries by giving business funds based on my experience in helping a Somalian grower through his application.

essays.prompt: How does the WBB program meet your educational and/or professional goals? (250 words)
essays.essay:
My parents sold a grand vision of my future; a future replete with white coats and stethoscopes. For a while, I bought into this idea because it made sense. Like any good physician, I loved digging into details, solving puzzles, and did well under pressure. Yet, I ventured into a shoe reselling business that inspired me to do more with entrepreneurship. I even tried to sell this idea back to my parents - “Business is a soft skill,” they’d say. So, doctor it was.

Heeding to their advice, I stashed my entrepreneurial spirit to the backlogs and instead, went all-in on biology. The summer before sophomore year, I interviewed and accepted an internship at a science-based incubation lab in Istanbul called Technopark.

Yet, my experience at Teknopark inadvertently led me back to business. I sat in financial board meetings, listened to supply chains discuss strategies to reduce overhead costs and grow towards profitability, and observed negotiations between manufacturers and startups. It was a lot to take in, but this internship enabled me to see that the development of new technologies are not always rooted in the name of science, but in the opportunity to grow a profitable business.

Travelling the world in WBB, I can’t wait to see how my prior beliefs will continue to change. Following my internship at Teknopark, I continued an internship at EY Istanbul. Just like the global business I partook in, I know that WBB will continue my journey for growth and discovery in business.

essays.prompt: Describe something outside of your intended academic focus about which you are interested in learning. (250 words)
essays.essay:
It's almost impossible to avoid the allure of computer sciences when you're living in the Valley, but it truly is an enjoyable experience where one would spend hours in analyzing and debugging lines of code with a big chunk of mathematics involved.

Even though I've always been a scientific research kind of gal, I've been trying to expand my skill set. For a few months now, I've been trying to learn programming languages with the aid of my father who is a great inspiration to me. I've watched him use his knowledge in computer sciences, and I've even picked up working with HTML5, CSS, JavaScript, Joomla, XAMPP, and app development.

As a future-oriented person, I know there really is no way around technology (or that there should even be), as innovation is required in the stable growth of every environment. I'm not just talking in the way of how we integrate the use of web and mobile applications in our casual day-to-days, but also in how technology is how we collate and verify our data.

With my work as a research officer in the Neuroscience Club at my high school and in some of my summer research intensives (Santa Cruz, University of Massachusetts), I've seen how technology itself is integral in how researchers analyze and present findings - even using custom apps to maximize work efficiency.

In the near future, I see myself mastering coding more, either in my own time or through some elective courses offered in USC.

essays.prompt: The National Academy of Engineering (NAE) and their 14 Grand Challenges go hand-in-hand with our vision to engineer a better world for all humanity. Tell us which challenge is most important to you, and why.
essays.essay:
Nuclear Fusion Challenge

While we have more energy sources than ever before, I believe the disparities in energy access across the globe are a primary source of conflict between nations and a cause of human suffering, especially in poor countries lacking reliable electricity. As the population continues to grow, the demand for coal, gas and oil will increase. Without a clean energy source, this will further exacerbate problems with climate change and pollution. Therefore, the Nuclear Fusion challenge is one of the most important challenges we as a society must tackle to alleviate suffering and promote global harmony.

Recently, I read a news article about how scientists and engineers at the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory repeated a nuclear fusion reaction in a lab, generating more energy than was initially required. This feat occurred less than a year after the first human-induced nuclear fusion reaction was achieved after decades of work by thousands of scientists worldwide.

Despite its promise, we still have a long way to go before we can fully harness nuclear fusion power for the world to benefit. There are many difficult scientific, engineering, and scaling challenges, but the potential rewards justify pursuing such a grand challenge. I believe we owe it to ourselves and future generations to develop clean, abundant energy for all humanity, helping to create a better world.

essays.prompt: Describe how you plan to pursue your academic interests (math and game design) and why you want to explore them at USC. (Inferred standard phrasing; source labeled it a why-major essay for the USC Interactive Media & Games program.)
essays.essay:
I have always loved to draw, almost from the same time I first learned how to ride a horse. I would scribble page after page, trying to draw the most beautiful horse I could imagine. I was proud of what I drew and loved sharing them with my parents. Math, on the other hand, did not come easily to me, and I actually hated doing Kumon math that my mom forced me to do every day. I struggled to see how math could be fun, as my dad told me, until I learned that math can be used to create beautiful and complex systems, just like drawing the most beautiful horse. I began to appreciate how math is all around us, whether we consciously think about it or not. Since my sophomore year in high school, I started tutoring kids in math, and this really solidified my interest when I saw kids' eyes glitter as they finally got unstuck from their math problems.

Last summer at UCLA, I took a 2-week game design program to experience how video games are made and met local game developers. Here, arts and math were combined to make some of the most awesome games. I loved the collaborative process of coming up with new ideas, designing the game environment, and seeing creations come to life.

The Interactive Media & Games programs offered by USC will allow me to combine my interests in math and game design to continue pursuing my love for both. I believe that my strong background in math and arts will make me a better game designer and an asset to the program. As artificial intelligence and augmented reality become more common, I can't wait to see how we can integrate them to create more innovative games in the future.

I am also passionate about using game design to create a positive social impact. I believe that games can be used to teach, inspire, connect people, and make a difference in the world.

I am confident that the USC Interactive Media & Games program is the perfect place for me to pursue my academic interests in math and game design. I am eager to learn from the world-class faculty and collaborate with other students at one of the most prestigious universities.

essays.promptLabel: Pursuing your academic interests at USC
essays.prompt: Describe how you plan to pursue your academic interests at USC. Please feel free to address your first- and second-choice major selections. (250 words)
essays.essay:
When being asked to write about the thing that inspires me as a budding undergraduate majoring in the field of neuroscience, I have always been quick to my feet and fingers in expressing my liking towards biology, medicine, anatomy, and psychology. Expressed through countless activities, fellowships, and internship programs in the past few years which I believe were useful stepping stones for a future career, I plan on taking the best classes offered in USC's curriculum. I'm also looking forward into experiencing the best of the Trojan spirit where me and my future classmates would weather all academic exercises with a sense of unity and excitement.

I would also take the professionalism I gained during my time in the Summer Research Intensives at the Markstein Cancer Research Lab of the University of Massachusetts (2017) where me and several students worked long hours in trying to develop cancer tumors in the guts of fruit flies. As a Trojan undergrad, I feel that I am truly well-equipped to engage myself in more advanced types of experiments under the strictest set-ups. I will also try to engage myself more fully with USC's state-of-the-art facilities, its access to the latest medical and research equipment, scientific journals, and numerous well-achieved lecturers.

I have no doubt USC is the perfect place for me to find and expound on strategic plans when it comes to future career decisions. And I hope I will be allowed to find new meaningful experiences and add color to the campus's already-vibrant surroundings.

essays.prompt: What is something about yourself that is essential to understanding you? (250 words)
essays.essay:
I flat-out do not believe in the phrase "jack of all trades, master of none". Or, at least, I don't want to be boxed in by such conditions. For the majority of my life, I have always tried to dip my toes in whichever activity I have found suitable for my growth and enjoyable to the point that I would seek advanced information and experiences on them.

I'm a teenager who effectively utilized my time with a lot of hospital, research, and healthcare work related activities. Challenging and time-consuming as these commitments may be, I have also found great joy in allotting time into learning classical Indian singing (10 years experience) and dancing (8 years). With the former, I have received a Carnatic Concert Competition Recognition and, as with the latter, a Bachelor of Dance from Art Society of Mumbai.

Aside from these two creative outlets, I have also learned how to use and enjoy fashion in creating unique and personal pieces of clothing using raw materials which I have sourced from markets, interior design stores, and local shops. I've also developed a passion for backpacking, hiking, and exploring landmarks in the hopes that I'd be a more worldly person, and I've been learning how to properly perform weight-training exercises to keep my body in as well-enough state as my mind.

With my resourcefulness and mindfulness, I try as much as possible to be as well-rounded in every fundamental skill set in order to outperform my age and societal limitations.

essays.prompt: Describe how you plan to pursue your academic interests and why you want to explore them at USC specifically. Please feel free to address your first- and second-choice major selections. (250 words)
essays.essay:
I can’t wait to apply my experiences to USC and start solving some of the puzzles I experience in my life. Travelling to Turkey has shown me the profound impacts of inflation firsthand, as much of my family must grapple with rising prices daily. It is sad to see how people and businesses, including my family in Turkey, have felt poorer now given the devaluing Turkish Lira year over year. I want to learn about why this happens and how it can be prevented. The Economic Foundations for Business course will provide me with some clues.

While inflation is certainly an interest, the intersection of global studies and business is where my heart lies. The interdisciplinary approach at USC via the open enrollment policy will allow me to not only take business classes but also help me venture into social policy, humanities and other areas that will be necessary to be a strong global leader that can create impact through and beyond business.

The importance USC gives to diversity with the Golden Globe as the symbol of international diversity is momentous to me. Given my internships abroad and interest in global business I cannot imagine myself anywhere else. USC’s diversity itself is a perfect reflection of the global hub that is LA, and I can’t wait to contribute to it through volunteering in ISA and events like Globefest.

As I explore the palpable Trojan spirit I can’t wait to find a place in USC, my new home away from home.

essays.prompt: Describe how you plan to pursue your academic interests and why you want to explore them at USC specifically. Please feel free to address your first- and second-choice major selections. (250 words)
essays.essay:
It's 2:00 a.m., I should be sleeping, but I'm wide awake, cruising the world through Google Street View. When I can't tour the canals of Amsterdam or streets of Mexico City in-person, I'll be under a blanket with an iPad and Google Maps - my favorite way to relax.

With USC's interdisciplinary approach, I look to turn this unbridled passion for traveling into meaningful global impact. Through my internships abroad, I've learned that business can be a medium for inspiring positive global change. USC's open enrollment policy will let me build on my experience by combining courses in both global studies and business. In addition, unique business offerings like the International Exchange Program that leverages USC's strong connections to foreign universities will provide an unmatched international experience.

Furthermore, my travels have also taught me about business and economic issues across the world. At USC, courses like Economic Foundations for Business will offer insights to problems such as the devaluation of the Turkish Lira that my family has experienced. Above all, I'll learn about even more global issues outside of just Turkey and be able to use business to find their solutions.

I'm excited for the possibility of learning business at USC, and eager to represent the Trojan spirit. I know USC's extraordinary community will prepare me to be an accomplished thinker, business leader, and bridge-builder and I hope to contribute to the USC community through the international student mentorship program or hosting informal cultural potlucks.

Now if you'll excuse me, I've got more streets to explore.

essays.prompt: The core purpose of The University of Texas at Austin is, To Transform Lives for the Benefit of Society. Please share how you believe your experience at UT-Austin will prepare you to Change the World after you graduate. (250-300 words)
essays.essay:
My dad travels to Texas almost monthly for work purposes. He always tells me how great it is there, and even suggests moving there, following the influences of our many family friends and cousins. His constant remarks about Texas made me curious, and I researched the universities in the state. I discovered UT-Austin and was amazed by the Computer Science program. The vast amount of research opportunities at UT-Austin in areas such as AI, Parallel Computing, and Natural Language Processing intrigued me as these were concepts that I had worked with extensively. I know that I will be able to contribute to the research efforts by providing my insights into these technologies.

The reason that I am attending college is to start a business with my two best friends, and after delving into various CS programs at many schools, I determined that UT-Austin will help me best achieve my goals of creating a company that will change the world. Ever since I was in the third grade, I looked up to influential businessmen like Steve Jobs and Bill Gates. I was astonished by their ability to create and sell outstanding products. My dream is to follow in their footsteps and invent an application that will revolutionize both physical and online transactions. I believe that programs such as the Longhorn Startup will guide me through the entrepreneurial process, making this dream come to life. Joining student organizations such as the Texas Product Engineering Organization and Texas Convergent will help me expand my network and build connections with people who have various backgrounds.

essays.prompt: Describe how your experiences, perspectives, talents, and/or your involvement in leadership activities (at your school, job, community, or within your family) will help you to make an impact both in and out of the classroom while enrolled at UT. (250-300 words)
essays.essay:
I opened my phone to read the news: "Due to COVID-19, no activities may be held in-person." As my Boy Scout troop's Senior Patrol Leader (SPL), uncertainty clouded my mind about how to lead the troop. Despite the setback, a spark of determination ignited within me. Leading my troop through these uncharted waters became my mission.

As SPL for my Boy Scout troop, I've had a fair share of leadership experiences that have sharpened my ability to deliver value and impact others both inside and outside of the classroom. I needed to think quickly and figure out a solution that would allow the troop to function during this period. One of my responsibilities as SPL was to manage the scouts who held important leadership roles within the troop, known as Positions of Responsibilities (POR). I adapted each POR's role to match the virtual environment to ensure a smooth transition. Additionally, I established an efficient method of contact with the adult leaders so that we could have volunteers to help with any necessary process. Furthermore, I utilized Zoom's breakout rooms feature to split scouts into their patrols during our weekly meetings. The scouts were able to bond, advance in rank, and learn new skills. The online meetings became a beacon of hope in the darkness caused by the pandemic. Finally, I organized virtual outings, allowing scouts to achieve their camping requirements and contribute to the community.

Through my experience, I learned how to become adaptable and resilient, embracing my role as a leader. I realized the importance of guaranteeing that every person in our troop needs to be connected and valued. The leadership skills I acquired through my journey will help me during my time at UT-Austin by fostering a sense of unification. With my prior experience, I hope to lead many initiatives and projects that can benefit a multitude of communities.

essays.prompt: Describe your significant activities, employment, and achievements, particularly those relevant to the study of computer science. Also describe your educational and career goals.
essays.essay:
Embarking on my computer science journey, I started with simple yet fulfilling projects—a calculator, a story game, and a password manager. These early creations, created using Python and Java, were my first steps into a world where coding met creativity.

I was eager to enhance the complexity of my creations, so I shifted my attention to web development. It was here that I found my true passion. I learned the intricacies of JavaScript—the single-threaded wonder. I dove deep into the inner workings of the event loop, understanding concepts like the heap, message queue, and more. I was amazed by the Just-In-Time compiler—the way it was able to run asynchronous code so elegantly.

The knowledge I acquired in web development gave me the confidence to compete in hackathons. I formed a group of four, and we spent countless months participating in national and international competitions. My previous experience in Python was essential to our success in these competitions as we used it to develop accurate machine-learning models. I strengthened my skills as a front-end developer, but also improved as a back-end engineer, creating API routes and database connections. As a result of our hard work, we won several competitions like the Congressional App Challenge and Technology Student Association. My experiences were crucial in shaping my understanding of collaborative development. I learned how to lead a software team and navigate the various challenges in the development process.

At the same time, I was determined to improve my critical thinking skills. I learned C++ and delved into various programming algorithms such as depth-first-search, flood-fill, Dijkstra's, greedy, and more. I participated in an international competitive programming competition called USACO, where I applied my algorithmic knowledge to create programs to solve a given problem. I understood how to break down these problems into simple components, a skill that I gained from hackathons. These competitions sharpened my analytical abilities and helped me develop logical reasoning which I know is a vital skill to my future success.

My journey couldn't only be about competitions and hackathons. I needed to make a real difference in my community by helping people. This desire led me to establish a private tutoring organization to teach younger students the fundamentals of programming so that they can discover their passion for computer science, just like I did. The one-on-one sessions were more than just teaching lessons—they were a safe space for the next generation of programmers to express their unique ideas and create fun projects. Witnessing their growth and excitement after turning the concepts they learned into working programs was fulfilling.

All my accomplishments and activities shaped me into not just a great software engineer, but a thinker, a problem-solver, and a mentor. As I aspire to join the Turing Scholars program, I am eager to explore research opportunities at UT Austin. I envision leveraging technology in a future business to make a global impact. I am confident that the Turing program will be a pivotal step in realizing my dreams.

essays.prompt: Why are you interested in the major you indicated as your first-choice major? (250-300 words)
essays.essay:
My first experience with web development began with React.js. I was building a sorting visualizer that helped people physically observe how sorting algorithms such as merge and bubble sorts worked. I spent countless hours writing the algorithms, coding the user interface, and integrating seamless transitions. When I ran the code and saw the array bars sort itself, the pure bliss I felt was indescribable.

I continued building new projects through high school and even accepted a role as an intern software engineer at a social media startup called Revoteen. There, I worked to create new features on the web application. My most impactful project was building a messaging platform for the company, which allowed our team to communicate with users. As I programmed the backend, I noticed flaws that prevented the code from running. This fueled me because it was my first real-world challenge with real implications. I debugged the code, loving every moment of it. It took hours, but something about "console.logging" each variable state onto the developer tools was very satisfying. I tracked down each value, identifying its purpose and finally, like a needle in the haystack, I found the culprit: a small code segment with two syntax errors. It was an easy fix at that point and I was able to ship the code into production for the chat feature to launch.

It's these moments that define my love for programming. I know my passion for Computer Science, coupled with UT Austin's extensive resources, will help me scale new challenges. UT Austin's emphasis on undergraduate research and internship opportunities will enable me to become a better thinker and a more astute programmer. The skills I will acquire here will undoubtedly guide me to make big things happen in this field and I'm readier than ever.

essays.prompt: Tell us your story. What unique opportunities or challenges have you experienced throughout your high school career that have shaped who you are today? (500-700 words)
essays.essay:
A few months ago, I learned about the butterfly effect, which is the idea that small events can shape a complex system. More specifically, I wanted to learn about the butterfly effect with respect to the current universe and timeline. I started to ponder on my life and remember the multitude of tiny events that shaped who I was as a person. Had these events not occurred, or even been altered slightly, I may not be here writing my essay to UT-Austin.

That time when I was five years old my parents bought me a piano, and they asked me whether I would play it or not. Had I not said "yes," I would never have played the piano. I would never have discovered the amazing musical community. I would never have studied for my ABRSM exam in high school. For months, I practiced for multiple hours perfecting and memorizing four complex songs. I needed to play these four songs sequentially without any break, meaning that if I made a mistake I would have to restart everything. The frustration I felt when I played F instead of E made me want to stop completely. The repetitive arpeggios and trills made my fingers work so hard that veins appeared from the joints. I couldn't even type a message on my phone after I finished practicing. Nevertheless, I did not stop. I could hear the final song in my head, and I needed to achieve that. I could not let my weak thoughts hinder my progress from accomplishing this goal. On some days I could not hang out with my friends at the movies, or play basketball at the park because I had to finish these songs. I made many sacrifices, but I regret none of them. My piano teacher commended my work, and I scored high on the exam.

Or the time I chose to join a short Discord call with my friend in the ninth grade. It was here where we discussed plans to start a web development club the following year so that other students could have the same experiences with programming as we did. We developed a year-long curriculum that covered everything from the basics of website creation to the intricacies of database management. We were a group of four students working together to build something that would make a large impact. Hosting national hackathons with hundreds of participants required dedication and planning. We spent days and nights contacting sponsors and reaching out to experienced judges. My face lit up when I saw the progression of each of our members. They went from not knowing what HTML was to coding flawlessly in JavaScript. Had I not joined this call, I would never have exercised my leadership skills to help countless students discover their passion in the field of web development.

Or the time I decided to call just one more number. During the pandemic, my friend and I observed many local businesses shutting down. Our favorite restaurants were closing, and we wanted to prevent this from happening. We reached out to over 200 local businesses in my city in the hopes that one of them would let us build a website for them. Nearing the end of our long list, we were certain that no one would enlist the help of a few high schoolers to help them out. We decided to call just one more number, and to our ultimate surprise, they accepted our offer. We stayed up late during nights on call trying to build the best possible website for this business. Had I not dialed one more number, I would have never developed both my entrepreneurial skills and my ability to work with a partner to lead a large project.

Or that time I said the words "wassup" to a complete stranger in my English class. That friendship we created helped me discover the field of robotics, and I joined his FTC team as a software member. My hardware knowledge was very limited, and I was unaware of the various parts such as the sonic hub and shaft coupler. Due to this, I didn't leave my comfort zone in software. During our season, all our software members quit, and it was just me. Many hardware members also went on vacation and were slightly inactive. I started coming everyday, even during our school breaks, and I started working on the hardware side of things. I learned how the drivetrain works, and even reassembled it completely. Breaking away from the confines of my computer screen, I utilized my hands to learn the other half of robotics. I expanded my skill set, and I gained new perspectives on the field of engineering. Had I not greeted my friend that day, I would have never acquired a love for robotics.

It's these small events, a simple "yes" or a decision to take one more step, that make me who I am. These are my butterfly effects.

essays.prompt: Our families and communities often define us and our individual worlds. Community might refer to your cultural group, extended family, religious group, neighborhood or school, sports team or club, co-workers, etc. Describe the world you come from and how you, as a product of it, might add to the diversity of the University of Washington. (300 words)
essays.essay:
Although I was born in the United States, my parents have always tried to raise me within the supplementary confines of my Indian ethnicity. This amalgamation of two cultures have led me into exploring not just the sciences but also the liberal arts where I turned into practicing and preserving the flair of my rich South-Asian culture side-by-side with my alignment to American lifestyle.

Aside from my extracurricular involvements which centered mostly in the field of medicine-related research, I go to great lengths to keep my schedule balanced and create time for personal activities that contribute to my physical and social well-being. My efforts and creative streaks can be represented through my 8 years of commitment to Indian classical dance and 10 years of practicing Indian classical singing. This experience instilled in me a sense of multiculturalism that continues to be a big part of my life.

In the part of my life focused on student-level healthcare operations, I've worked with many researchers with different nationalities. These opportunities also remind me how the American social and corporate atmosphere greatly highlights inclusivity, which constantly reinvigorates my curiosity and openness when it comes to other cultures. This also shows very well in my school and neighborhood, where we boast having a lot of second-generation immigrants, refugees, and veterans. I've then had some time put in as a volunteer in a Veterans Affairs hospital where I've experienced the cultural and generational gaps with those who are my age and those who fought for our country.

In Washington, I aspire to do just the same - taking with me my determination of learning about new cultures and local customs while sharing my personal core principles of curiosity and harmonic, diplomatic nature.

essays.prompt: Our families and communities often define us and our individual worlds. Community might refer to your cultural group, extended family, religious group, neighborhood or school, sports team or club, co-workers, etc. Describe the world you come from and how you, as a product of it, might add to the diversity of the University of Washington.
essays.essay:
The famous roleplaying game, Dungeons and Dragons, invited me to a new community brewing of creativity and comfortability. Before being invited to try out this game, DND was just another silly game that was viewed to be "nerdy." However, little did I know that by joining my friend that fateful day on a call with 4 others I was unfamiliar with, I would find my community.

My initial thoughts shifted from a minor curiosity to an invested love for the game. From the diverse character creation to the wide range of paths to take, DND can bring you to any world. That was one of the qualities I appreciated the most. Just the opportunity to run far, far away to a place only in your imagination motivated me to get back into the arts.

It wasn't just the game itself that was fun, it was the people that took part that brought it all to life. Every run-in with a puzzle or a monster, we collaborated to find the way out. I built strong relationships with these people that I'll forever hold close to me. These people allowed a growth of empathy and allowed me to take in different perspectives and appreciate the benefits and flaws. I've learned through these peers that there is a depth to DND not many are aware of; this game makes communities.

At the University of Washington, I hope that with these experiences I can weave my knowledge into the diversity of the Huskies. My experiences with DND align with the problem-solving, explorative, and collaborative views held up by the university. Though many will end at different destinations after the adventures, it's the journey that matters most. I hope that my adventures will start here at the University of Washington.

essays.prompt: Tell a story from your life, describing an experience that either demonstrates your character or helped to shape it. (500 words)
essays.essay:
Through the Community Psychology Team at the University of California Santa Cruz, I conducted extensive research examining the relationship between social psychology and social empowerment in kids. From the moment seven select students walked into the room during the summer of 2018, I was gleaming with pride and joy, amazed with their excitement to learn and investigate. My work with Latinx 4th and 5th graders as part of the Youth Participatory Action Research program had been a constant reminder for me to never lose the child-like wonder and delight when it comes to scientific discoveries, big or small.

At the end of the program, the student researchers were eager to make a mural of all the community values they had acquired in the past month. I remember how the girls fought over pink versus blue paint and how the boys argued over whether the mural should depict a race car or a butterfly. What amazed me was how, in the end, they decided on a blue butterfly, which they felt best represents change, hope, and inclusivity.

As I watched the children paint every detail, I was struck by their commitment. Watching them work together sparked a new curiosity within me that I could barely contain. At night, I lay awake thinking about the different theories of psychology that I had learned - Rogers's Theory of Experimentalism or Bandura's Social Learning Theory - and realized that I was just recalling the names of theories and beliefs which have always justified my own choices and behavior. As was natural to me, I immediately yearned to learn more.

Building upon this interest in psychology, I joined a different research project at UC Santa Cruz - one focusing primarily on neuroscience. There, I learned about the migration and differentiation of different neurons as they related to specific conditions - namely, ALS and Autism.

I would sometimes then become frustrated with how slow the research process was. I kept asking myself, "How could I make the process go faster?", "What are the possible variables that need to be adjusted?", "What am I doing wrong?"

Then, it hit me: this experience of failing and pushing forward against all unfortunate hurdles encountered taught me how researchers get personally involved in their studies and, while the tasks seem taxing in certain degrees, it's all in the greater service of mankind. I was again reminded of how the student researchers from the previous year who inadvertently rekindled my sense of curiosity were trying, in their own ways, to build a future we can share while genuinely caring for each other.

While my research on mice brains never guaranteed everyday success, I pushed forward and got into the habit of maintaining the level of curiosity I began with. Perhaps, I even ended up with more. As I enter college, it would be these lessons of exploration, curiosity, and community which I hope would help me succeed as a future healthcare provider, eager to discover new things about myself, my community, and the world.

essays.prompt: Tell a story from your life, describing an experience that either demonstrates your character or helped to shape it.
essays.essay:
"Pong!"
I sigh, looking at the unwinnable hand in front of me. My mom had already claimed my first unwanted tile on my opening turn, setting herself up with a hand that was likely to win the game.

We were playing Mahjong again, the fifth time this week. This complex, unassuming game is all about strategy—bringing in a tile, throwing out a tile, trying to create a winning pattern. It requires you to know when to let go of something, even if it's tempting to keep it.

As I took another glance at the broken hand in front of me, I couldn't help but feel hopeless, much like in the other aspects of my life. The pandemic had completely disrupted my routine, and worst of all, my mom had been diagnosed with lymphoma in the liver. For a while, I was perplexed at the chaotic mess that laid in front of me—missing assignments, unwashed clothes, and crumpled tissues littering my bedroom floor. These habits became a pattern of behavior, seeping into every corner of my life. Much like a player with a broken hand in Mahjong, I had removed myself from the activities, commitments, and routine that made me, me.

It did not take me long to realize that I was playing with a hand that did not work. Held captive by my subpar habits, I put off things that were meant to be done ages ago, which only fueled my frustration and self-doubt. I told myself I would get it done "later," except that "later" never actually came. I wasted hours overindulging in content that I convinced myself was essential to distract from my mom's diagnosis. I was pushing everything away, and only when I was faced with my own stagnation, did it finally dawn on me: I needed to change, and that began with discarding harmful tiles.

One by one, habit by habit, I began to add worthwhile tiles to my hand, discovering how much more I could achieve by doing so. One tile stood out among the crowd: the daily practice of peeling fruits for my family. I found solace in the process, redirecting that previously negative energy into this more therapeutic activity. Every day, I challenged myself to peel better than the previous day, striving for improvement. Another tile I added to my hand was the ability to start opening up to others. I began to have conversations with my parents about the things I had long neglected to tell them, like how I learned to take pictures of a patient's eyes, or the latest gossip about a group at my school. With friends, the unusual gap between us had started to close as I freed up time to meaningfully connect. Whether it be listening to music together or catching up over Trader Joe's chips and dips, the relationships I built were strengthening. Little by little, a winning hand had unconsciously started to form.

This winning hand presented itself in many aspects of my daily life, offering changes in not just my routine, but also my perspective. I joined and created clubs at my school, striving to practice the newfound skills I acquired. I explored my passion for healthcare, volunteering at hospitals and doing pediatric and optometry internships. I took on basketball and flag football, eager to make more meaningful connections. Those new tiles in my hand were continuously being developed and sharpened the more I used them.

So as I sat across from my mom, staring at her neatly arranged tiles, I couldn't help but find parallels in this game we've grown to treasure. As I play, I am reminded of the power of knowing it is okay to let go, using your discarded tiles as stepping stones to a brighter future.

essays.prompt: Tell us why you decided to apply to the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In addition, please include why you are interested in studying the major(s) you have selected. If you selected undecided please describe your areas of possible academic interest. (up to 650 words)
essays.essay:
Badgers have always reminded me of bigger weasels or maybe a scruffy raccoon. In all honesty, the only times I've seen a badger was on the internet, or at the San Diego Zoo. Even so, they only have honey badgers, they are not the same as American badgers. However, these tumbling, silly mammals taught me something when I first searched them up. Spiritually, these animals represent perseverance along with having resilience against hardships. I wish I had known how to be a badger when I faced the tyranny of choices when it came to my future.

The spring of 2023 only brought a weight of impending doom that was to settle on my shoulders. I had completed my second to last year in high school, yet I was met with a plethora of paths to take. At some point I wanted to be an astronaut, then I wanted to be a doctor, then a neuroscientist, then an emergency cardiac surgeon, then a chef. However, with every new career choice in mind, I quickly fell back into the unknown. I didn't know who I was going to be, and it terrified me to the core. When it came to choosing the hobbies I wanted to explore, I could not charge in like a badger would. But with one experience at a university, I persevered down that path and I haven't looked back since.

The UCLA Game Design program caught my interest the first time I saw it in the mail. Sure, I played games and it was a huge hobby of mine, why not look at it from a different perspective I thought. When the time came when I moved my bags into my temporary dorm, I was not prepared for the deep dive this experience would take me. Every lecture fueled the fire and the love for not only game development but also computer science. This sent me down the path and I tumbled into programs centered around software engineering. For once, this wasn't just a temporary interest in a career, this was a full-blown forest fire that consumed my every move. With this, I felt honed in and focused. I felt resilient to the stress of picking and choosing what I wanted to do with my life.

The University of Wisconsin-Madison fuels the fire of computer science - it's that same fire I hope to catch with mine. Harboring a broad range of computer science courses, with many collaborative opportunities and a strong set of student organizations, the University of Wisconsin-Madison has the tools to not only build the fire but to keep it burning. A student organization that caught my eye was WACM, or ACM's Women in Computing. As a fellow woman myself, this immediately brought a comforting feeling that there are so many out there following the same path I'm traveling down. Not only am I fascinated by the Linux content provided, but it facilitates many opportunities for others to connect about technology. Bringing social aspects to a very independent set of work is a key part of what makes WACM such a nurturing community. The weekly social events allow students to build strong and resilient bonds, just like badgers.

Now, I may not have fur or whiskers or claws like badgers, but I know that the journey of finding what I want to do in the future comes with the skill of resilience and perseverance. University of Wisconsin-Madison raises students to be just like badgers, to be resilient, and to persevere through challenges. Not saying I physically want to be a badger. Though I wish I could be a part of the strong community built by the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

essays.promptLabel: Identity, culture, or background and personal growth (dare to grow)
essays.prompt: Vanderbilt University's motto, Crescere aude, is Latin for "dare to grow." In your response, reflect on how one or more aspects of your identity, culture, or background has played a role in your personal growth, and how it will contribute to our campus community as you dare to grow at Vanderbilt (250 words).
essays.essay:
As the son of a Turkish mother and Dutch father, yet living in America, my life feels like a conundrum. Born on American soil, there's no doubt I'm American, except that until preschool the only languages I responded to were a mix of Turkish and Dutch. Travelling to Turkey and the Netherlands over 14 times each, there's no doubt I'm an international native, except that I've never lived outside the US. Quite simply, I'm an outsider.

While I'll never have both feet into one community, I'm okay with that. Rather than wallow about what I can't change, my goal has been to build the bridges between these aspects of my life. When the Turkey/Syria earthquakes struck, I helped my community abroad by rallying my school community at home in a fundraiser. When I joined an internship at EY in Istanbul, I made friends in my community abroad by talking about eccentric interests from my community at home like pokemon cards and cosplay. The important thing to connect people is acknowledging that people aren't “better” than each other, they are just different.

Over the years, I've continued to grow outside the labels that define me. While travelling abroad has always been about visiting family, since high school I have taken advantage of this opportunity to explore internships. At home, I've continued to redefine my creative process, experimenting with woodchippers and eventually partnering with Recycleballs nonprofit to turn discarded tennis balls into stress relievers. At Vanderbilt, conundrums (differences) are celebrated. I hope to be the bridge-builder who unites my fellow students, hosting informal get togethers and exploring the creative options to unite Vanderbilt's students just like I explore the world. Whether I am Turkish, Dutch, or American, I look forward to making Vanderbilt my new home away from home!

essays.prompt: Virginia Tech's motto is "Ut Prosim" which means 'That I May Serve'. Share how you contribute to a community that is important to you. How long have you been involved? What have you learned and how would you like to share that with others at Virginia Tech? (120 words)
essays.essay: When I had first joined a local math tutoring center, the one my mom paid for, I was the one being tutored. Immediately I grew accustomed to the warm energy brought into the single room building. Years and years passed; I learned the basics of algebra to the complicated theories of calculus. The month of March rolled by the year 2021, the one tutor at the center stopped me after class. She then offered me a job to be a tutor for the younger kids. This was the opportunity I've never thought I'd receive, yet I immediately grabbed it. Every week from that point on, I'd come in to tutor kids from 4th to 9th grade.

essays.prompt: Tell us about something that really sparks your intellectual interest and curiosity and compels you to explore more. It could be an idea, book, project, cultural activity, work of art, start-up, music, movie, research, innovation, question, or other pursuit. (250 words)
essays.essay:
Aside from my adamant love of biology and other sciences, I have always been fascinated and inspired by classic literature. Mainly, I am much focused into reading Gothic Literature and my all-time favorite would be Mary Shelley's The Modern Prometheus - more commonly known as 'Frankenstein'.

First published anonymously in 1818, the very content and intent of the classic are still relevant to this day and age, inspiring many movies, spiritual sequels, and artistic endeavors. But what continuously captivates me is the active spirit in which Frankenstein's monster, through all the sorrow he had, had pressed on.

"Life, although it may only be an accumulation of anguish, is dear to me, and I will defend it."

Shelley's timeless quote rings loudly to me. It is a beautiful statement on how a person (with or without a soul) continues to strive living happily and in comfort, despite so many things going awry.

Also very notable is the protagonist Victor's remorse in his scientific and outdated alchemical approach into bringing into this world the perfect human specimen. To me, this work of fiction reflects the dream of trying to "perfect" humanity's conditions and is a warning tale about how we should all pursue our dreams with caution.

From both tragic characters, I have learned that life in itself is precious in its current state and how we, as budding researchers and future scientists, must ever try to study all the ways to improve it in ways that do not endanger our very spirit.

essays.prompt: What was the most influential factor in your decision to apply to Whittier? (500 words)
essays.essay: I decided to apply to Whittier because as I was researching colleges I discovered that Whittier has a good social science program and I'm going to be a Sociology major. I want to be able to learn about the way people function as a whole and how that can take effect in modern society and I'm determined to find the best place to study and learn. I also think that the location is perfect for where I want to attend college as well as the campus is gorgeous. It isn't too far away from home, but far enough where I could be independent and look after myself without my mom peering in. I've also always enjoyed Southern California, whether it was going down to look at colleges or I was on vacation with family so I think it could be a great place to live. I also enjoy that Whittier has a smaller campus, which means that the school has a lower teacher to student ratio. At my current high school our class sizes are too big to be able to get to know and talk to teachers often, and so I hope to attend a smaller school so I can form those bonds with my professors and be able to ask questions whenever I need. With that being said, I never liked the idea of just being a statistic so knowing that my attendance would represent me as a person rather than a number is something that I find reassuring.
